Brain flexibility associated with need for cognition contributes to creative achievement

Psychophysiology. 2019;56:e13464. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.13464

All functional imaging data are freely available for re-
search from the International Neuroimaging Data‐Sharing 
Initiative (http://dx.doi.org/10.15387/ fcp_indi.retro.slim). 
Specifically, 164 participants (70 male) with both imaging 
data and NFC scores were included in this study, and some 
of them (N = 100) also completed the Creative Achievement 
Questionnaire (CAQ). All participants were Han, aged from 
17 to 26 years old, the mean was 19.99 ± 1.12. We used two 
exclusion criteria to ensure imaging data quality: (a) three 
participants were excluded whose maximal head motion 
between volumes in any direction was > 3 mm or rotation 
in any axis > 3° during scanning, (b) all participants exhib-
ited relatively few bad volumes (defined as any volume with 
framewise displacement (FD) value > 0.5 mm) that ranged 
from 0 to 9.91%; thus, no one was excluded according to the 
widely used criterion based on > 10% bad volumes. Through 
self‐report questionnaires and structured and semistructured 
interviews, none had a history of psychiatric illness, cogni-
tive disorders, substance abuse, or MRI contraindications. 
The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee 
of the Brain Imaging Center of Southwest University, and 
written informed consent was obtained from each participant.

All imaging data were collected on a Siemens 3T Trio scanner 
(Siemens Medical Systems, Erlangen, Germany). Resting-
state fMRI data were obtained with gradient echo‐planar 
imaging (EPI) sequences: repetition time (TR) = 2,000 ms, 
echo time (TE) = 30 ms, field of view (FOV) = 220 × 220, 
flip angle = 90°, slices = 32, thickness = 3.0 mm, slice 
gap = 1.0 mm, voxel size = 3.4 × 3.4 × 4 mm3. This scanning 
lasted 8 min and contained 242 volumes; all participants were 
instructed to close their eyes and rest but not to fall asleep.

The fMRI data were preprocessed using the advanced 
Data Processing Assistant for Resting‐State fMRI (DPARSF, 
http://www.rfmri.org/DPARSF; Yan, Wang, Zuo, & Zang, 
2016; Yan & Zang, 2010), which is based on Statistical 
Parametric Mapping (SPM, http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/
spm). The first 10 volumes were discarded to suppress the 
equilibration effects and consider subjects’ adaptation to 
the environment. The remaining volumes were slice‐timing 
corrected, realigned, and spatially normalized to the MNI 
(Montreal Neurological Institute) template and resampled to 
3 × 3 × 3 mm3. Then, we conducted a series of noise clean-
up strategies, including wavelet de‐spiking, nuisance signal 
regression, and data scrubbing. Specifically, the performance 
of wavelet de‐spiking has been shown to be superior to the 
standard de‐spiking algorithms, and the default parameters 
were used, which were equivalent to prior studies (Patel et al., 
2014). Nuisance signals including white matter, cerebrospi-
nal fluid, and head motion parameters and their derivatives 
using the Friston 24‐parameter model were regressed out 
to control the potential influence of physiological artifacts 
(Friston, Williams, Howard, Frackowiak, & Turner, 1996). 
We further implemented data scrubbing to better address 
head motion concerns. The bad time points were regarded as 
regressors that defined as volumes with FD Power > 0.5 mm 
as well as the two succeeding volumes and one preceding 
volume to reduce the spillover effect of head motion (Power, 
Barnes, Snyder, Schlaggar, & Petersen, 2012). In addition, 
linear and quadratic trends were also included as regressors 
since the BOLD signal exhibits low‐frequency drifts. We 
next conducted spatial smoothing with 4‐mm full‐width at 
half‐maximum Gaussian kernel and band‐pass temporal fil-
tering (0.01–0.1 Hz). Finally, given that no consensus has 
been reached on global signal regression (GSR) in fMRI 
studies (Caballero‐Gaudes & Reynolds, 2017; Liu, Nalci, & 
Falahpour, 2017), we performed preprocessing with and 
without GSR, and the results of GSR are represented in the 
online supporting information, Appendix S1.

2.5 | Dynamic network construction
A graph is made up of nodes and edges in graph theory 
analysis. For node definition, we employed a 264‐node 
functional atlas that is widely distributed across the whole 
brain and includes 13 large‐scale brain networks (Power 
et al., 2011), as shown in Figure 1a. We chose Power 264 
regions of interest (ROIs) for several reasons. First, the 
creation of 264 putative functional areas was based on 
resting‐state FC in healthy young adults, which is consist￾ent with the data type and sample population in this study. 
Second, our main focus was to examine the relationship 
between the flexibility of a large‐scale brain network and 
behavior. The putative 264 ROIs contain many subgraphs 
(13 well defined) in good agreement with known func￾tional brain systems and are significantly more similar to 
the functional systems than those in other templates (e.g., 
the 90‐parcel AAL atlas; Power et al., 2011). In addition, 
we hoped to be consistent with existing research on brain 
flexibility in the selection of templates (Chen et al., 2016; 
Mattar et al., 2015). Considering that signal intensity may 
be poorer in certain locations of the brain, 11 nodes with 
lower BOLD signal strength were identified and discarded 
(Wig, Laumann, & Petersen, 2014); thus, 253 nodes were 
reserved. The time series of each node was acquired by 
averaging the BOLD signals from all voxels in this region, 
and the Pearson correlation of the time series between pairs 
of nodes was calculated to represent the edges (i.e., FC). 
A sliding window approach was used to construct a dy￾namic FC matrix for each participant. We considered that 
small and large windows have been associated with a nar￾row range of network flexibility values across the brain, 
while medium time windows (e.g., 75 s and 100 s) have 
uncovered a wide range of network flexibility (Telesford 
et al., 2016). Meanwhile, given one TR is 2 s in this study 
and needs more windows to track dynamic trajectories, the 
window length was therefore set to 50 TRs and the time 
gap of each window was set to 1 TR, yielding 183 overlap￾ping time windows to capture the temporal fluctuations in 
FC during a short period, and then Fisher's z transformation 
was conducted to improve normality.

2.6 | Multilayer community detection
To explore the spatiotemporal segregation of nodes in dy￾namic FC, we connected the adjacent time windows by 
adding interlayer connections (temporal link) between each 
node and itself in the adjacent window (Bassett et al., 2011; 
Mucha et al., 2010), as shown in Figure 1b. Then, a gen￾eralized Louvain algorithm was used to find the putative 
functional modules based on the optimization of the mod￾ularity quality function (Mucha et al., 2010). Intuitively, 
nodes have dense connections within modules but sparse 
connections between modules. The optimal multilayer 
modularity quality was based on the relative densities of

The structural resolution parameter determines the number of 
modules within a given layer, and the temporal resolution pa￾rameter controls the consistency of modules detected across 
layers (Bassett et al., 2013). To avoid the deviation from the 
results of multilayer community detection (Bassett et al., 
2013; Telesford et al., 2016), while considering the simplifi￾cation of calculations and the consistency with previous re￾search, we used the common default values that set = =1
(Bassett et al., 2011, 2013; Bassett, Yang, Wymbs, & Grafton, 
2015; Telesford et al., 2016). In addition, because the com￾munity detection algorithm is vulnerable to near‐degenera￾cies (Good, de Montjoye, & Clauset, 2010) and stochastic 
elements in this algorithm (Blondel, Guillaume, Lambiotte, & 
Lefebvre, 2008), the output usually varies from run to run. 
We therefore performed the multilayer community detection 
algorithm 100 times to yield optimized partitions of the mul￾tilayer modularity for each time (Bassett et al., 2011, 2013).

2.7 | Node, network, and global flexibility
The results of the generalized Louvain algorithm are shown 
in a partition matrix (nodes × layers), in which elements 
represent the community assignment of node i in layer l, as 
shown in Figure 1c. The multilayer modularity quality func￾tion simultaneously and optimally assigned brain regions to 
communities in all layers so that community labels are con￾sistent across layers, thus avoiding the community matching 
problem (Bassett et al., 2011, 2013). Based on the optimal 
community partition, node flexibility can be defined as the 
rate at which each node changes the assigned community be￾tween two consecutive time layers (Bassett et al., 2011), that 
is, the actual changing times divided by possible changing 
times. A value close to 1 indicates that a node's community 
assignment is highly variable. Network flexibility and global 
flexibility can also be defined as the mean flexibility of the 
nodes within the network or across the whole brain (Bassett 
et al., 2011). We calculated the flexibility values separately 
for each community detection and averaged across 100 
optimizations.
